nodes.name: Ikshvaku
nodes.description: Eldest son of Vaivasvata Manu and first king of Ayodhya, founder of the Solar dynasty (Suryavamsha) into which Rama was born. He is named once in the Rig Veda, and the epics and Puranas trace the whole Ikshvaku line from him. Through his son Nimi he is also counted as the ancestor of the kings of Videha.
nodes.story: The Vishnu Purana says Ikshvaku was born from the nostril of Manu when he sneezed. He became king at Ayodhya and had a hundred sons. Once, preparing the ancestral rites of the ashtaka, he sent his son Vikukshi to the forest to hunt meat for the offering. Tired and hungry on the way back, Vikukshi ate a hare from the bag. When the meat was brought for the rite, the family priest Vashishtha declared it defiled, because part of it had already been eaten. Ikshvaku banished his son for the lapse, and Vikukshi became known as Shashada, 'the hare-eater'. After Ikshvaku died, Shashada came back and ruled Ayodhya righteously, so the line continued through him. The Bhagavad Gita remembers Ikshvaku as a link in the royal chain of teaching: Vivasvan taught the eternal yoga to Manu, and Manu taught it to Ikshvaku.
variations: The Vishnu Purana has him born from Manu's sneeze (kshuta). Other texts simply list him as the eldest of Manu's sons.
The Puranas name Vikukshi-Shashada as his heir. Valmiki's genealogy gives his son as Kukshi, followed by Vikukshi.
The Puranas make Nimi, founder of the Videha line of the Janakas, a son of Ikshvaku. Valmiki's genealogy of Janaka starts from Nimi without linking him to Ikshvaku.

nodes.name: Mandhata
nodes.description: A universal emperor (chakravartin) of the Ikshvaku line, son of King Yuvanashva, famous for his unusual birth and for conquering the whole earth. The Rig Veda names Mandhatri as someone the Ashvins helped. Later texts treat him as the model of a generous, sacrificing king.
nodes.story: King Yuvanashva had no son and went to the forest, where the sages performed a rite for him. They consecrated a vessel of water charged with mantras, meant to make his queen conceive. That night the king woke up burning with thirst and drank the water, not knowing what it was. As a result he himself became pregnant. In time the child was born from his side. When the sages wondered who would nurse the baby, Indra put his own finger into its mouth and said, 'He shall suckle me' (mam dhasyati). So the boy was named Mandhata. He sucked nectar from the god's finger and grew with amazing speed. He went on to conquer the world 'from where the sun rises to where it sets', performed a hundred sacrifices, and married Bindumati, daughter of Shashabindu. Their sons included Purukutsa and Muchukunda.
variations: In Valmiki's genealogy (Bala Kanda 70) Mandhata comes after Trishanku and Dhundhumara. In the Puranas Trishanku is a much later descendant of Mandhata.
Some manuscripts of the Uttara Kanda say Mandhata was killed by the demon Lavana, who held Shiva's trident. Buddhist Jatakas tell a separate story of Mandhata's endless desire.
The Puranas say Mandhata's fifty daughters all married the aged sage Saubhari.

nodes.name: Trishanku
nodes.description: An Ikshvaku king who wanted to enter heaven in his own body. Cursed by the house of Vashishtha, he was raised skyward by Vishvamitra, who made a new heaven for him. He hangs upside down among the stars, and 'Trishanku's heaven' has become a byword for being stuck between two worlds.
nodes.story: Trishanku asked his priest Vashishtha to perform a sacrifice that would lift him to heaven in his own body. Vashishtha refused. The king then went to Vashishtha's hundred sons, who were angry that he had gone over their father's head. They cursed him to become a chandala, an outcaste, dark-skinned and dressed in iron ornaments. In this state Trishanku asked Vishvamitra for help. Vishvamitra agreed and began the rite, but the gods would not come to accept their shares. So by the power of his own austerities he sent the king up toward heaven. Indra threw him back down, head first. 'Stop!' cried Vishvamitra, and held Trishanku in mid-air. Then, in fury, the sage began to create a second universe with its own seven sages and constellations. The gods gave in: Trishanku would stay, shining upside down, in a heaven of stars made for him alone.
nodes.abode: Trishanku Svarga (a heaven of stars made by Vishvamitra)
variations: In Valmiki the curse comes from Vashishtha's hundred sons. In the Harivamsha, Prince Satyavrata is exiled by his father Trayyaruna for carrying off a bride. He later kills and eats Vashishtha's cow during a famine, and Vashishtha names him Trishanku for his 'three sins'.
The Puranas make him the son of Trayyaruna and father of Harishchandra, many generations after Mandhata. Valmiki's genealogy puts a Trishanku before Mandhata and does not mention Harishchandra.
During the famine of his exile Satyavrata fed Vishvamitra's abandoned family. This explains the sage's loyalty to him.

nodes.name: Harishchandra
nodes.description: An Ikshvaku king who is the lasting ideal of truthfulness in Hindu tradition. In the Aitareya Brahmana he promises his son to Varuna, which leads to the story of Shunahshepa. The Puranas tell how Vishvamitra tested his truth by taking everything he had.
nodes.story: In the Markandeya Purana, Harishchandra once rashly offended Vishvamitra and then, to make amends, gave the sage his entire kingdom. The sage also demanded a sacrificial fee (dakshina) and gave him a month to pay it. Harishchandra would not break his word. In Kashi he sold his queen and young son to a brahmin as servants. Then he sold himself to a chandala who kept the cremation ground. There, as its watchman, he collected shrouds and fees from the dead. One night his wife came carrying their son, who had died of a snakebite. She had no money for the fee. Harishchandra recognised them, but he would not waive the fee he owed his master. Husband and wife prepared to die together on the pyre. At that moment Dharma, Indra and the gods appeared and revealed it had all been a test. The boy was brought back to life, and Harishchandra rose to heaven with his people.
variations: The Aitareya Brahmana calls him Vaidhasa, son of Vedhas. The Puranas make him the son of Trishanku (Satyavrata).
The Vedic story is about his vow to Varuna and the ransom of Shunahshepa. The long ordeal of truth under Vishvamitra comes later, in the Markandeya and Devi Bhagavata Puranas.
The Markandeya Purana says Vashishtha was so angered by Vishvamitra's treatment of Harishchandra that the two sages cursed each other into birds and fought (the Adi-Baka battle).
His queen is called Shaivya in the Sanskrit Puranas and Taramati in later regional retellings and dramas.

nodes.name: Taramati (Shaivya)
nodes.description: Queen of Harishchandra and mother of Rohita(shva). She shares every stage of her husband's ordeal of truth. The Sanskrit Puranas call her Shaivya; the name Taramati comes from later regional retellings, dramas and films.
nodes.story: When Harishchandra could not pay the fee Vishvamitra demanded, Shaivya was the one who told him to sell her so that his word would stand. She was sold to a brahmin in Kashi and led away with her little son Rohitashva, doing hard work as a household servant. One day the boy was bitten by a snake while picking flowers and grass, and he died. Alone at night, Shaivya carried him to the cremation ground. She did not recognise the ragged watchman who demanded the burial fee. When at last husband and wife knew each other by her cries and the marks on the child, neither of them asked to break the bond of servitude. Instead they built a single pyre to die on together. Her faithfulness shared in the triumph that followed: the gods revealed the test, and the child woke up alive.
symbols: half a garment offered as fee (regional retellings)
sources: Regional Harishchandra dramas and kavyas (Kannada, Telugu, Tamil, Marathi)
variations: Shaivya is her name in the Markandeya and Devi Bhagavata Puranas. Taramati (or Chandramati in the South) appears in medieval regional literature and folk theatre.
In many regional versions she tears off half of her only sari to pay the cremation fee. This detail is not in the Sanskrit Puranas.

nodes.name: Rohita
nodes.description: Son of King Harishchandra. He was born by Varuna's grace on condition that he be sacrificed to the god, and he escaped by fleeing into the forest. His substitute was Shunahshepa. In the Puranas, as Rohitashva, he is the child who dies and is revived at the end of Harishchandra's ordeal.
nodes.story: Harishchandra had a hundred wives but no son. Following Narada's advice he prayed to Varuna, promising to sacrifice the son he would be given. Rohita was born, and the king kept putting Varuna off: until the boy was ten days old, until he had teeth, until he wore armour. When Rohita came of age and heard of the vow, he took his bow and went into the forest. Each year, as he started for home, Indra met him in human form and sang the song of wandering: 'The fortune of one who sits, sits too; it lies down when he lies down; it moves when he moves. Keep moving (charaiveti)!' For six years Rohita wandered. Meanwhile Varuna had struck his father with dropsy. In the sixth year Rohita met the starving brahmin Ajigarta. He bought Ajigarta's son Shunahshepa for a hundred cows, to be offered in his own place.
variations: The Puranas call him Rohitashva and make him the ancestor of Harita, Champa (founder of Champapuri) and eventually Bahu, father of Sagara.
The Bhagavata Purana tells the Vedic sacrifice story briefly. The Markandeya Purana adds his death by snakebite and revival.
Local tradition links him with the founding of Rohtas and Rohtak. This connection is not in the Sanskrit texts.

nodes.name: Shunahshepa
nodes.description: A brahmin boy sold by his father to be sacrificed in place of Prince Rohita. He was freed when he praised the gods, and Vishvamitra adopted him as Devarata. The Rig Veda speaks of Shunahshepa bound to the sacrificial posts, and tradition names him as the seer of hymns 1.24–30.
nodes.story: Ajigarta was a starving brahmin. He sold his middle son Shunahshepa to Prince Rohita for a hundred cows, as a substitute victim for Varuna. At Harishchandra's royal consecration no one would bind the boy to the post. Ajigarta did it himself for another hundred cows, and then took up the knife for a third hundred. Seeing that he was about to be slaughtered 'as if he were not human', Shunahshepa turned to the gods. He praised Prajapati, Agni, Savitr, Varuna, the Vishvedevas, Indra and the Ashvins, each of whom sent him on to another god. Finally he praised Ushas, the Dawn. With each verse to her one fetter loosened, and with the last the bonds fell away and Harishchandra's dropsy was cured. Shunahshepa then refused to go back to his father. Vishvamitra, who had been the hotr priest, took him on his lap as his son, naming him Devarata, 'god-given'.
variations: In the Valmiki Ramayana the sacrificer is King Ambarisha of Ayodhya and the boy is the middle son of the sage Richika. Vishvamitra teaches him two hymns to Indra and Upendra (Vishnu), and Indra frees him.
The Aitareya Brahmana says that fifty of Vishvamitra's sons refused to accept Shunahshepa as their elder and were cursed. The Bhagavata repeats this.
Scholars debate whether the Brahmana story was built out of the Rig Vedic references or preserves an older legend.

nodes.name: Sagara
nodes.description: An Ikshvaku emperor whose sixty thousand sons were burned to ashes by the sage Kapila while searching for his sacrificial horse. The ocean (sagara) is said to be named after the chasm they dug. Their liberation became the task of his descendants, ending with Bhagiratha bringing the Ganga down to earth.
nodes.story: Sagara had two queens, Keshini and Sumati, the sister of Garuda. The sage Bhrigu granted that one would bear a single son to continue the line and the other sixty thousand. Keshini bore Asamanja. Sumati bore a gourd that burst into sixty thousand infants, who were raised in jars of ghee. Years later Sagara began a horse sacrifice. Indra, in disguise, stole the horse and hid it in the underworld. At their father's command the sixty thousand princes dug down through the earth, splitting it open until the regions of the world cried out. In the depths they found the horse grazing beside the meditating sage Kapila. Thinking he was the thief, they ran at him with weapons. Kapila opened his eyes and uttered a sound, and all sixty thousand were reduced to ashes. The chasm they had dug later filled with the Ganga's waters and became the ocean, sagara.
sources: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Tirtha-yatra: Sagara and Bhagiratha)
variations: Valmiki calls him the son of Asita, and the sage Chyavana blesses his pregnant mother. In the Puranas he is the posthumous son of Bahu, born with the poison (gara) a co-wife gave his mother, and raised in the hermitage of Aurva.
The Puranas say he conquered the Haihayas, Shakas and Yavanas. Vashishtha persuaded him to spare them and instead impose distinctive hairstyles on them.
The Bhagavata says the princes died because of their own sin in insulting Kapila, not because of the sage's anger.

nodes.name: Asamanja
nodes.description: Son of Sagara and Queen Keshini, and father of Anshuman. Sagara banished him for cruelty to the children of Ayodhya. The Bhagavata Purana explains this conduct as a yogi's deliberate pretence.
nodes.story: Asamanja was the one son of Sagara's queen Keshini, the heir promised by Bhrigu's boon. But as he grew up he became a terror to the city. According to Valmiki he would seize the children of Ayodhya, throw them into the Sarayu river, and laugh as they drowned. The citizens came to Sagara and asked him to choose between his son and his people. The king put the good of his subjects first and banished his own son from the kingdom. Asamanja's son, the gentle and brave Anshuman, stayed at court, won the love of everyone, and became his grandfather's heir. The Bhagavata remembers Asamanja differently. It says he had been a yogi in a former life and acted cruelly on purpose so that he would be sent away from worldly life. Before leaving, he used his yogic power to bring the drowned children back to life.
variations: Valmiki and the Mahabharata present him simply as wicked. The Bhagavata makes him a former yogi who pretended to be cruel and revived the drowned children.
Some Puranas also call him Panchajana.

nodes.name: Anshuman
nodes.description: Grandson of Sagara through Asamanja. He found the lost sacrificial horse and, by his humility before Kapila, learned how his burned uncles could be saved. He ruled after Sagara and spent his last years in austerities, trying without success to bring the Ganga down.
nodes.story: When the sixty thousand princes did not come back, Sagara sent his grandson Anshuman to follow their path underground. Anshuman bowed to the elephants that hold up the four quarters, and each blessed his journey. At last he found the horse, and beside it the heap of ashes that had been his uncles. He wanted to offer water for their souls but could find none. Then Garuda, their mother's brother, appeared. He told Anshuman that ordinary water would not do: only the Ganga, the river of heaven, could purify them and send them to heaven. In the Bhagavata, Anshuman also praised Kapila with deep reverence, and the sage gave him the horse. Anshuman brought the horse back so that Sagara could finish the sacrifice. As king, and later as a hermit in the Himalayas, he tried for the rest of his life to bring the river down, but never succeeded.
variations: In Valmiki, Garuda (Suparna) tells Anshuman that the Ganga is needed. In the Bhagavata and Vishnu Purana, Kapila himself gives the horse and the advice after Anshuman praises him.

nodes.name: Dilipa
nodes.description: Son of Anshuman and father of Bhagiratha. Like his father, he tried in vain to bring the Ganga down to earth. The name also belongs to a later king of the same line: Kalidasa's Dilipa, father of Raghu, whose service to the cow Nandini opens the Raghuvamsha. The two are often merged in popular memory.
nodes.story: Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha tells the best-known story of a Dilipa. He was a perfect king, but he had no child. He and his queen Sudakshina went to the hermitage of their guru Vashishtha, who saw the cause by meditation. Once, returning from Indra's heaven, Dilipa had hurried past the divine cow Surabhi without saluting her, and she cursed him to be childless until he served her offspring. So the king became a cowherd to Nandini, Surabhi's daughter. For twenty-one days he followed her through the forest, resting when she rested. Then a lion, a servant of Shiva, sprang on her. Dilipa's arm froze as he reached for an arrow. So he offered his own body to the lion in the cow's place. The lion vanished: it had been Nandini's test. Pleased, she granted him a son, Raghu.
variations: Valmiki and the Puranas give a Dilipa as the son of Anshuman and father of Bhagiratha. He tried for thirty thousand years to bring the Ganga down and died of illness without succeeding.
Kalidasa's Dilipa, husband of Sudakshina and father of Raghu, is usually identified with a later king: Khatvanga-Dilipa of the Puranas, who is said to have gained liberation in a single muhurta.
Valmiki's genealogy has no Dilipa as Raghu's father. There Raghu is the son of Kakutstha.

nodes.name: Bhagiratha
nodes.description: Son of Dilipa and great-great-grandson of Sagara. Through immense austerities he brought the celestial Ganga down to earth and into the underworld to liberate his sixty thousand ancestors. The river is called Bhagirathi after him, and a 'Bhagiratha effort' means a superhuman labour.
nodes.story: Bhagiratha left his kingdom with his ministers and did severe austerities at Gokarna, fasting and standing among five fires. Brahma, pleased, granted him the Ganga. But he warned that the earth could not bear the force of her fall, and only Shiva could. So Bhagiratha worshipped Shiva for a year, standing on one toe. Ganga came down proudly, meaning to sweep Shiva into the underworld. Instead he caught her in his matted locks and held her there for years, until Bhagiratha's prayers made him release her in seven streams. Bhagiratha drove ahead in his chariot, and the river followed him across the land. When she flooded the sacrificial ground of the sage Jahnu, he drank her up, and released her only when the gods pleaded with him. At last the Ganga followed Bhagiratha down to Patala, washed over the ashes of Sagara's sons, and they rose to heaven.
variations: Valmiki places his austerities at Gokarna. Later tradition places them at Gangotri in the Himalayas, where a rock is shown as Bhagiratha's seat.
In the Bhagavata, Ganga worries that sinners will pollute her. Bhagiratha replies that saints bathing in her will purify her again.
Valmiki's genealogy makes Kakutstha his son. The Bhagavata gives Shruta.

nodes.name: Raghu
nodes.description: Ikshvaku king whose fame gave the line one of its names, Raghuvamsha. This is why Rama is called Raghava, Raghunatha and Raghupati. Kalidasa made him the hero of cantos 3–5 of the Raghuvamsha, where he conquers every direction and then gives away everything he owns.
nodes.story: At the end of his conquest of the world, Raghu performed the Vishvajit sacrifice, in which a king gives away all his possessions. He was left with only clay vessels. Just then the young scholar Kautsa arrived. He needed fourteen crore gold coins as the fee for his teacher Varatantu. Raghu welcomed him with water in an earthen pot, and Kautsa realised the king had nothing left. He turned to leave. But Raghu would not let a seeker leave his door with nothing, and he decided to take the wealth from Kubera, lord of riches, by force. He slept that night in his war chariot, ready to march at dawn. In the morning his treasurers reported that gold had rained into the treasury overnight. Raghu pressed all of it on Kautsa, and Kautsa would take no more than his teacher's fee. As he left, Kautsa blessed the king with a son like himself: Aja.
symbols: clay vessel of the Vishvajit sacrifice
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 70 and Ayodhya Kanda 110
variations: Valmiki makes Raghu the son of Kakutstha and father of Pravriddha (Kalmashapada). The Vishnu Purana and Kalidasa make him the father of Aja.
Kalidasa makes him the son of Dilipa and Sudakshina. The Bhagavata and Vishnu Purana make him the son of Dirghabahu, son of Khatvanga (Dilipa).
In the Raghuvamsha the young Raghu fights Indra, who had stolen Dilipa's hundredth sacrificial horse. Indra then grants the merit of the sacrifice.

nodes.name: Aja
nodes.description: King of Ayodhya, the son of Raghu in Kalidasa and the Vishnu Purana, and father of Dasharatha, which makes him Rama's grandfather. Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha tells of his winning Indumati at her svayamvara and his inconsolable grief at her sudden death.
nodes.story: On his way to Princess Indumati's svayamvara in Vidarbha, Aja shot a wild elephant that attacked his camp. It turned out to be the gandharva Priyamvada, freed by the arrow from a curse, who gave Aja the Sammohana weapon in gratitude. At the svayamvara Indumati passed by king after king and placed the garland on Aja. He beat the jealous rivals with the stupefying weapon. Years of happy marriage followed. One day, while they were in a garden, a heavenly garland fell from the vina of Narada as he flew overhead. It landed on Indumati's breast, and she died at once. Aja's lament over her is one of the most famous passages in Sanskrit poetry. Vashishtha sent word that she had been a cursed apsara whose exile had now ended. Aja stayed only until young Dasharatha could rule. Then he gave up his body at the meeting of the Ganga and the Sarayu, and joined her.
sources: Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 70 and Ayodhya Kanda 110
variations: Valmiki's genealogy makes Aja the son of Nabhaga, not Raghu. Kalidasa and the Vishnu Purana make him Raghu's son.
The svayamvara, the death of Indumati and Aja's lament are Kalidasa's telling. The epics only list Aja as Dasharatha's father.

nodes.name: Indumati
aliases: Harini (her former life as an apsara)
nodes.description: Princess of Vidarbha, sister of King Bhoja, who chose Aja at her svayamvara and became the mother of Dasharatha. She is known mainly from Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha, where she is an apsara living under a curse, and her death is the occasion of Aja's lament.
nodes.story: Kalidasa describes Indumati's svayamvara as a procession of kings. Her maid Sunanda leads her along the row of assembled suitors and describes each one: the lord of Magadha, the king of Anga, the ruler of Avanti, the kings of Mathura and Kalinga. As Indumati passes each suitor, his face falls, and Kalidasa compares her to a moving lamp-flame that lights up each mansion on a highway and then leaves it dark. She stops before Aja of Ayodhya and places the madhuka garland on his neck. Years later, a divine garland falling from Narada's vina struck her, and she died. Then the truth was told. She had been the apsara Harini, sent by Indra to break the sage Trinabindu's austerities. The sage cursed her to be born as a mortal until she saw a heavenly flower. Her death was the end of that exile.
sources: Padma Purana (Indumati as Ayu's queen, a different figure)
variations: Indumati as Aja's queen comes from Kalidasa (c. 5th century CE). The epics do not name Dasharatha's mother.
The Padma Purana gives the name Indumati to the wife of King Ayu of the Lunar line. That is a different figure.

nodes.name: Ila
nodes.description: Child of Vaivasvata Manu who changes sex between female (Ila) and male (Sudyumna). As Ila she bore Pururavas to Budha, so the Lunar dynasty is called Aila after her. In the Rig Veda, Ila/Ida is a goddess of the sacrificial offering, and Pururavas is called Aila; the Shatapatha Brahmana describes Ida rising from Manu's offering after the flood.
nodes.story: Manu had no children and held a sacrifice to Mitra and Varuna for a son. His wife Shraddha secretly asked the priest for a daughter, and the offering produced a girl, Ila. At Manu's request Vashishtha turned her into a man, Sudyumna. One day, while hunting, Sudyumna rode into a grove at the foot of Meru. Long before, Shiva had said, to please Parvati, that any man entering that grove would become a woman. So the prince, his companions and even his horse all changed. As Ila she wandered until Budha, son of the Moon, saw her and loved her, and she bore him Pururavas. Vashishtha then prayed to Shiva, who granted a compromise: Sudyumna would be a man for one month and a woman the next. As a man he fathered sons who ruled the east. At last he handed the throne to Pururavas and went into the forest.
variations: Shatapatha Brahmana: Ida rises from Manu's offering of butter and curds after the flood and calls herself his daughter. There is no change of sex.
Valmiki Ramayana: Ila is a male king, son of Kardama Prajapati, who enters a grove where Shiva is playing with Uma. Uma grants that he will be a man and a woman in alternate months.
Puranas: Ila is born a daughter because the priest's rite went wrong, is made male (Sudyumna) by Vashishtha, and changes sex again in Shiva's grove.
Some texts say Ila is both father and mother of Pururavas. Traditions differ on whether the Vedic goddess Ida and Manu's child are the same figure.

nodes.name: Pururavas
nodes.description: First king of the Lunar dynasty, son of Budha and Ila, who ruled from Pratishthana. His love for the apsara Urvashi is one of the oldest love stories in the world: it appears as a dialogue in Rig Veda 10.95, is told in full in the Shatapatha Brahmana, and is the subject of Kalidasa's play Vikramorvashiyam.
nodes.story: The apsara Urvashi agreed to live with Pururavas on conditions. He was never to let her see him naked, and her two pet rams were to be kept safe. The gandharvas missed her in heaven and stole the rams one night. Pururavas leapt up to chase the thieves without stopping to dress. The gandharvas sent a flash of lightning, Urvashi saw him naked, and she vanished. The king wandered in grief until he found her at a lotus lake, swimming with other apsaras in the shape of swans. In the Rig Vedic hymn he begs her to come back, and she answers, 'Pururavas, do not die... there are no friendships with women; their hearts are the hearts of hyenas.' Still, she allowed him one night each year. The gandharvas eventually granted him a place among them, and taught him to kindle the sacred fire that would carry him there.
variations: The Mahabharata says that in his pride Pururavas robbed brahmins and was destroyed by the sages' curse.
In Kalidasa's play he first wins Urvashi by rescuing her from the demon Keshin. She is cursed into a vine, and he gets her back with a magic gem.
The Bhagavata makes Pururavas the one who divides the single Vedic fire into three.

nodes.name: Ayu
nodes.description: Eldest son of Pururavas and Urvashi and heir to the Lunar throne at Pratishthana. He was the father of Nahusha. An Ayu is named in the Rig Veda, and the epics and Puranas make him the link between Pururavas and Nahusha.
nodes.story: The Mahabharata and Harivamsha remember Ayu mostly as a link in the chain of kings. He married Prabha, daughter of Svarbhanu, and had five sons: Nahusha, Kshatravriddha, Rambha, Raji and Anenas. The Padma Purana adds a story about how his heir was born. Ayu and his queen had no son. So the king went to the sage Dattatreya, who lived like a wild ascetic among wine and women to test those who came to him. Ayu served him patiently and was not put off by how he appeared. Dattatreya was pleased and gave him a fruit for his queen, promising a son devoted to Vishnu. The demon Hunda wanted to stop the birth. He had been told the son of Ayu would kill him. So he stole the newborn Nahusha, but the child was saved and raised in the hermitage of Vashishtha. There he grew up to kill Hunda and marry Ashokasundari.
variations: The Mahabharata and Harivamsha name his wife as Prabha, daughter of Svarbhanu (the eclipse demon Rahu). The Padma Purana calls her Indumati, daughter of Svarbhanu.
Scholars debate whether the Rig Vedic Ayu is the same figure as Pururavas's son. The Rig Vedic hymn 10.95 mentions Urvashi's son but does not name him.

nodes.name: Nahusha
nodes.description: Lunar king, son of Ayu and father of Yayati. He was raised to the throne of Indra while Indra was in hiding, grew arrogant, and was cursed by Agastya to fall to earth as a python. The Mahabharata uses him as the classic example of pride destroying merit, and tells how Yudhishthira freed him.
nodes.story: After killing Vritra, Indra was polluted by the sin of brahmin-slaying and hid in a lotus stalk. The gods made the virtuous king Nahusha their new Indra. But power corrupted him, and he demanded Indra's queen Shachi. On Brihaspati's advice Shachi set a condition: he must come to her in a palanquin carried by the great sages. Nahusha harnessed the rishis to his litter. Impatient, he kicked Agastya on the head and shouted 'Sarpa! Sarpa!' ('Move! Move!'). 'Sarpa' also means 'serpent', and Agastya cursed him to become one. Nahusha fell from heaven as a huge python. Ages later, in a forest, the python caught Bhima and held him, powerless. Yudhishthira came looking for his brother. The python asked him who a true brahmin is and what should be known. Yudhishthira answered wisely, and the curse ended. Nahusha took his heavenly form and rose to the sky.
sources: Rig Veda (Nahusha, as a king and people)
variations: In the Anushasana Parva version, the sage Bhrigu hides in Agastya's matted hair and is the one who curses Nahusha.
The Padma Purana says he killed the demon Hunda and married Ashokasundari, daughter of Shiva and Parvati.
Some retellings say it was the Saptarishi who carried the palanquin. The Mahabharata speaks of the brahmin sages generally.

nodes.name: Yayati
nodes.description: Lunar emperor, son of Nahusha, husband of Devayani and Sharmishtha, and father of five sons whose lines include the Yadavas and the Pauravas (later the Kurus). Cursed with early old age, he borrowed youth from his son Puru. His story is the Mahabharata's great lesson that desire is never satisfied by being indulged.
nodes.story: Yayati married Devayani, daughter of Shukracharya, and promised never to take her servant, the asura princess Sharmishtha, to his bed. But he secretly fathered three sons with Sharmishtha. When Devayani found out, she ran to her father. Shukra cursed Yayati to become old at once, but allowed him to pass the old age to a son who would accept it. Yadu, Turvasu, Druhyu and Anu all refused, and Yayati cursed each of them. The youngest, Puru, took his father's old age without complaint. For a thousand years Yayati enjoyed the pleasures of youth. Then he gave Puru back his youth, together with the kingdom, saying: 'Desire is never quenched by enjoyment; like fire fed with ghee, it only blazes higher.' He went to the forest, rose to heaven by his austerities, and fell again when he boasted about them.
nodes.vahana: chariot (a gift of Indra, in the Puranas)
variations: The Mahabharata (Adi 81–88) says he fell from heaven for pride and was stopped mid-fall by his daughter Madhavi's sons: Ashtaka, Pratardana, Vasumanas and Shibi. They gave him their merit.
In the Bhagavata he tells Devayani the parable of the he-goat and the she-goat, and they both reach liberation.
Some Puranas say Indra gave him a divine chariot, which passed down to the Pauravas and later to Janamejaya.

nodes.name: Devayani
nodes.description: Proud daughter of Shukracharya, preceptor of the asuras. She fell in love with Kacha, and when he rejected her she became Yayati's chief queen. Her sons Yadu and Turvasu founded the Yadava and Turvasu lines.
nodes.story: One day the asura princess Sharmishtha and her friends were bathing, and Devayani was with them. Indra, in the form of a wind, mixed up their clothes on the bank, and Sharmishtha put on Devayani's garment. When Devayani objected, Sharmishtha taunted her as the daughter of a priest who begged at her father's door. Then she pushed Devayani into a dry well and left her there. King Yayati was out hunting, heard her cries, and pulled her out by her right hand. Because he had taken her hand, she later claimed him as her husband. Devayani refused to go home. Shukracharya threatened to leave the asuras altogether, so King Vrishaparvan agreed to her price: Sharmishtha and a thousand maids would serve her for life. So Devayani married Yayati with her rival as her servant. That arrangement led to Yayati's secret union with Sharmishtha and to his curse of old age.
variations: Some Puranas name her mother as Jayanti, daughter of Indra. The Mahabharata does not name her mother.
Retellings differ on how much she is to blame. The Mahabharata presents her as proud but wronged, and the Bhagavata ends her story with her renouncing the world.

nodes.name: Sharmishtha
nodes.description: Danava princess, daughter of the asura king Vrishaparvan. She became Devayani's servant to protect her people, and secretly became the wife of Yayati. Her son Puru inherited the throne and founded the Paurava line, from which the Kurus and Pandavas came.
nodes.story: Sharmishtha had pushed Devayani into a well in a quarrel. Shukracharya threatened to abandon her people, and the asuras depended on his knowledge of how to revive the dead. So Sharmishtha gave up her rank and agreed to be Devayani's lifelong servant, following her into Yayati's household. Some time later, in the asoka grove where she lived, she approached the king. She argued that a servant's master is the husband of her mistress, and that turning away a woman in her season is a sin. Yayati could not refuse, and she bore him three sons: Druhyu, Anu and Puru. When Devayani discovered who their father was, her anger led to Shukra's curse on Yayati. In the end Sharmishtha's youngest son, Puru, was the one who took on his father's old age, and it was her line, not Devayani's, that inherited Yayati's kingdom.
variations: The Mahabharata presents her giving up her rank as noble self-sacrifice for her people. Later retellings, such as V. S. Khandekar's novel Yayati, make her the more sympathetic heroine.

nodes.name: Kacha
nodes.description: Son of Brihaspati, sent by the gods to learn the Mritasanjivani, the knowledge of reviving the dead, from Shukracharya. He succeeded despite being killed three times by the asuras. He refused Devayani's love, and the two cursed each other.
nodes.story: Kacha became Shukracharya's disciple and served him and his daughter Devayani faithfully for a thousand years. The asuras saw what he was after and killed him again and again, but each time Devayani's tears moved her father to bring him back to life. The third time, they burned Kacha, mixed his ashes into Shukra's wine, and the sage drank it. Unable to revive him without killing himself, Shukra taught the life-restoring knowledge to Kacha inside his own belly. Kacha burst out, and then used the knowledge to revive his teacher. Shukra then forbade wine to all brahmins. When Kacha's training was complete, Devayani asked him to marry her. He refused, because she was his guru's daughter and so like a sister to him. She cursed him that his knowledge would never work for him. He cursed her that no brahmin would ever marry her. He then taught the knowledge to others.
variations: In the Mahabharata, Kacha replies that her curse cannot stop him from teaching the knowledge, so it will still work through his students.
Some retellings and plays end with reconciliation between Kacha and Devayani. This is not in the epic.

nodes.name: Yadu
nodes.description: Eldest son of Yayati and Devayani. Yayati cursed his line never to hold sovereign kingship after Yadu refused to take his father's old age. He is the ancestor of the Yadavas, the Haihayas and, through Shurasena and Vasudeva, of Krishna. The Rig Veda names Yadu and Turvasha together as tribes or chiefs.
nodes.story: When Shukra's curse withered Yayati, he turned first to his eldest son. 'Take my old age, Yadu, and give me your youth for a thousand years.' Yadu refused. He could not bear white hair, a sagging body, and the loss of the pleasures of youth. Yayati cursed him: his descendants would never be crowned as sovereign kings. For this reason, the Puranas say, Krishna would later refuse the throne of Mathura. Yadu went to rule in the south-west, and his descendants became the Yadavas. The Bhagavata remembers him more gently. It says that while wandering, King Yadu met a carefree young avadhuta. When Yadu asked where his joy came from, the ascetic, later identified as Dattatreya, told him about the twenty-four gurus of nature, from the earth and the python to the honeybee. Yadu listened and gave up attachment.
nodes.abode: South-western lands (towards the Charmanvati and Vetravati); Mathura region
sources: Bhagavata Purana, Canto 9, ch. 18–23 and Canto 11, ch. 7–9
variations: Texts disagree about what the curse meant. Some say his line would have no kingdom at all. Others say only that its rulers would not be consecrated as emperors, and the Yadavas continued to rule as chieftains and republics.
His sons Sahasrajit and Kroshtu founded the Haihaya and the Vrishni-Andhaka branches. Krishna comes from Kroshtu's line.

nodes.name: Puru
nodes.description: Youngest son of Yayati and Sharmishtha. He alone accepted his father's old age, and was rewarded with the central kingdom over his elder brothers. He founded the Paurava dynasty of Dushyanta, Bharata, Kuru and the Pandavas. The Purus are a leading tribe in the Rig Veda.
nodes.story: Yayati's four elder sons refused to take his old age. Then he turned to Puru, the youngest, born of the servant-queen Sharmishtha. Puru said at once, 'I will do as you command, father,' and took on the weight of years. For a thousand years he lived as an old man while his father enjoyed youth. When Yayati was ready to go to the forest, he gave Puru back his youth. Then he announced that Puru would be his heir. The citizens and brahmins protested: why should the youngest son pass over Yadu, grandson of Shukra himself? Yayati explained that a son who obeys his father is his true heir, and that Shukra had approved it. The people accepted, and Puru was crowned at Pratishthana. From him came the Pauravas, the line of Dushyanta, Bharata and Kuru.
variations: In the Rig Veda the Purus are a powerful tribe, sometimes allied with the Bharatas and sometimes their rivals (e.g. in the Battle of the Ten Kings, RV 7.18). Later genealogies make both lines descend from Puru.
The Puranas list the Paurava succession between Puru and Dushyanta differently.

nodes.name: Dushyanta
nodes.description: Paurava king who married Shakuntala by the gandharva rite in the hermitage of Kanva, and later denied her. He is the father of the emperor Bharata. The Brahmanas name him only indirectly, through Bharata's patronymic Dauhshanti. His story is told in the Mahabharata and dramatised in Kalidasa's Abhijnanashakuntalam.
nodes.story: Hunting deep in the forest, King Dushyanta came to the hermitage of the sage Kanva on the Malini river. There he met Kanva's foster-daughter Shakuntala and fell in love with her. Kanva was away, so they married by the gandharva rite of mutual consent, and the king promised that her son would be his heir. He went back to his capital and did not send for her. Years later Shakuntala came to his court with their son. In the Mahabharata, Dushyanta denies ever having known her, afraid of what his subjects would think. She replies with a long speech on a wife's dignity and a son's worth. Then a voice from the sky declares that the boy is his. Dushyanta embraces them both, saying he had only wanted the truth proclaimed publicly. He names the boy Bharata, 'the one to be supported'.
nodes.abode: The Paurava capital (later tradition places it at Hastinapura)
sources: Shatapatha Brahmana 13.5.4 (as father of Bharata Dauhshanti)
variations: In Kalidasa's play, Durvasa's curse makes Dushyanta genuinely forget Shakuntala. The ring he gave her is lost in a river and found in a fish's belly, which restores his memory.
Kalidasa ends the play with Dushyanta fighting demons for Indra and being reunited with Shakuntala in the celestial hermitage of Marica (Kashyapa).
The Puranas differ about his father, for example Ilina or Raibhya.

nodes.name: Shakuntala
nodes.description: Daughter of the sage Vishvamitra and the apsara Menaka, raised by the sage Kanva. She married King Dushyanta and was the mother of the emperor Bharata. The Shatapatha Brahmana already names an apsaras Shakuntala as Bharata's mother. The Mahabharata tells her story in full, and Kalidasa's play made her the most famous heroine in Sanskrit drama.
nodes.story: Indra feared Vishvamitra's austerities and sent the apsara Menaka to distract him. Their union produced a daughter, whom Menaka left on the banks of the Malini. Shakunta birds sheltered the infant until the sage Kanva found her, and he named her Shakuntala after them. She grew up in his hermitage and married King Dushyanta. When she brought their son to court, the king claimed not to know her. Shakuntala did not beg. She told him that a wife is half of a man, that a son is himself reborn, and that truth outweighs a thousand horse sacrifices. If he would not accept her, she said, her son would still rule the earth. A heavenly voice confirmed her words. In Kalidasa's version the sage Durvasa, ignored by the lovesick girl, curses her to be forgotten by the one she is thinking of. Only the lost ring can break the curse.
nodes.abode: Kanva's hermitage on the Malini river
variations: The Shatapatha Brahmana calls her an apsaras who conceived Bharata at Nadapit.
Durvasa's curse, the lost ring and the reunion in Marica's heavenly hermitage come from Kalidasa. They are not in the Mahabharata, where Dushyanta knowingly denies her.
The Padma Purana version is close to Kalidasa's play.

nodes.name: Bharata (son of Dushyanta)
nodes.description: Son of Dushyanta and Shakuntala, a universal emperor after whom the Bharata lineage (and, in many texts, Bharatavarsha, India) is named. The Shatapatha and Aitareya Brahmanas praise Bharata Dauhshanti for his countless horse sacrifices. He is the ancestor of Kuru and the Pandavas.
nodes.story: Raised in Kanva's hermitage, Shakuntala's son was so strong as a child that he tied lions, tigers and elephants to the trees around the ashram and rode on their backs. The hermits called him Sarvadamana, 'tamer of all'. In Kalidasa's play he forces open the mouth of a lion cub to count its teeth. After Dushyanta accepted him, he was named Bharata and in time became a chakravartin. The Brahmanas say he performed horse sacrifices beside the Ganga and the Yamuna, and that no king before or after could match his deeds, 'as no mortal can touch the sky with his arms'. The Puranas add a sad story. Bharata's queens killed their own sons because he said the children did not look like him. With his line in danger, he held a sacrifice to the Maruts, and they gave him Bharadvaja as an adopted heir.
nodes.abode: The Paurava capital (later tradition places it at Hastinapura)
variations: Many Puranas (e.g. the Bhagavata, Canto 5) say Bharatavarsha is named after a different Bharata, the son of Rishabha. Others name it after Dushyanta's son.
In the Mahabharata his son is Bhumanyu, and the line continues from father to son. The Puranas insert the adopted Bharadvaja (Vitatha).
The Aitareya Brahmana says the sage Dirghatamas Mamateya performed his great consecration (aindra mahabhisheka).

nodes.name: Kuru
nodes.description: Paurava king, son of Samvarana and Tapati (daughter of Surya). The Kuru dynasty and the sacred field of Kurukshetra are named after him. He is the ancestor of Pratipa, Shantanu, and so of both the Kauravas and the Pandavas.
nodes.story: King Kuru went to a stretch of land and began to plough it himself with a golden plough, drawn by Shiva's bull and Yama's buffalo. Indra came down and asked what he was doing. Kuru answered that he was cultivating the eight virtues there: austerity, truth, forgiveness, compassion, purity, charity, yoga and celibacy. Indra laughed and went away. But Kuru kept ploughing day after day. At last Indra came back and offered him a boon. Kuru asked that anyone who died on that ground, whether fasting or fighting bravely, would go straight to heaven. Indra granted it. The field became Kurukshetra, the 'field of Kuru', also called Dharmakshetra, the field of dharma. Generations later his descendants would fight the great war there. The Mahabharata remembers his line simply as the Kurus.
variations: The detailed story of ploughing with Shiva's bull and Yama's buffalo is in the Vamana Purana. The Mahabharata tells the origin of Kurukshetra more briefly.
The Kurus as a people appear in late Vedic literature (Kuru-Panchala). The individual king Kuru is known from the epic and the Puranas.

edges.label: Ikshvaku was the eldest son of Vaivasvata Manu
edges.variation: The Vishnu Purana says he was born from Manu's sneeze

edges.label: Manu passed the eternal yoga, received from Vivasvan, on to Ikshvaku (Bhagavad Gita 4.1)
Vashishtha was family priest (purohita) of Ikshvaku and his line
Mandhata, son of Yuvanashva, descends from Ikshvaku
edges.variation: Puranic line: Ikshvaku - Vikukshi - Kakutstha - ... - Yuvanashva - Mandhata. Valmiki's list is Ikshvaku - Kukshi - Vikukshi - Bana - Anaranya - Prithu - Trishanku - Dhundhumara - Yuvanashva - Mandhata

edges.label: Through his son Nimi, Ikshvaku is ancestor of the Janakas of Videha (Puranas)
edges.variation: Vishnu Purana 4.5 and the Bhagavata make Nimi Ikshvaku's son. Valmiki starts Janaka's genealogy from Nimi without linking him to Ikshvaku

edges.label: Trishanku (Satyavrata), son of Trayyaruna, descends from Mandhata through Purukutsa
edges.variation: Valmiki's genealogy reverses this and puts Trishanku before Mandhata

edges.label: Indra fed the newborn Mandhata from his own finger and gave him his name ('he shall suckle me')
The Rig Veda (1.112.13) praises the Ashvins for helping Mandhatri
Vishnu, appearing in the form of Indra, taught Mandhata the duties of kings (Mahabharata, Shanti Parva 64–65)
Harishchandra was the son of Trishanku (Satyavrata)
edges.variation: The Aitareya Brahmana calls Harishchandra the son of Vedhas (Vaidhasa). Valmiki's genealogy has no Harishchandra

edges.label: The house of Vashishtha cursed Trishanku: Vashishtha's hundred sons turned him into a chandala
edges.variation: In Valmiki (Bala Kanda 58) the curse comes from Vashishtha's sons, not from Vashishtha himself. In the Harivamsha, Vashishtha names Satyavrata 'Trishanku' for his three sins

edges.label: Vishvamitra became Trishanku's priest, sent him up bodily toward heaven, and created a new heaven of stars for him
Indra threw Trishanku out of heaven head first, refusing him entry in his mortal body
Rohita was born to Harishchandra by Varuna's grace (Aitareya Brahmana)
Taramati (Shaivya) was Harishchandra's queen and shared his ordeal of truth
Varuna granted childless Harishchandra a son, on condition that the son be sacrificed to him
Varuna struck Harishchandra with dropsy for failing to give up Rohita as promised
Narada taught Harishchandra the verses on the value of a son and advised him to pray to Varuna (Aitareya Brahmana)
Vishvamitra was hotr priest at Harishchandra's sacrifice (Aitareya Brahmana). In the Puranas he tests the king's truthfulness by stripping him of everything
edges.variation: The ordeal of truth comes from the Markandeya and Devi Bhagavata Puranas

edges.label: Vashishtha was Harishchandra's family priest and brahman priest at the Shunahshepa sacrifice. He took the king's side against Vishvamitra (Markandeya Purana)
After the ordeal, Indra and the gods raised Harishchandra to heaven together with his subjects (Markandeya Purana)
Dharma, who had disguised himself as the chandala master, revealed the test and blessed Harishchandra
edges.variation: The Markandeya Purana names Dharma personified. Identifying Dharma with Yama is traditional but not explicit in the text

edges.label: Shaivya (Taramati) was the mother of Rohita(shva), whose death and revival end the ordeal
Varuna claimed Rohita as his promised sacrificial victim, and Rohita fled to the forest
Indra, in human form, urged the wandering Rohita each year to keep moving ('charaiveti')
Rohita bought Shunahshepa for a hundred cows to be sacrificed in his place
Sagara descends from Rohita through Harita, Champa, Sudeva, Vijaya, Bharuka, Vrika and Bahu (Puranas)
edges.variation: Valmiki has no Rohita. There Sagara is the son of Asita, in the line of Mandhata's descendants

edges.label: Vishvamitra adopted the freed Shunahshepa as his eldest son, renaming him Devarata
edges.variation: Adoptive father. His birth father was Ajigarta (Aitareya Brahmana) or Richika (Valmiki)

edges.label: Bound to the sacrificial post, Shunahshepa praised Varuna, the god who had claimed the victim (Rig Veda 1.24–25)
As Shunahshepa praised Ushas, his fetters loosened verse by verse and fell away (Aitareya Brahmana)
Shunahshepa praised Agni in several of his hymns of deliverance
Shunahshepa praised Savitr, who sent him on to Varuna
Shunahshepa first turned to Prajapati, who sent him on to Agni
In the Valmiki Ramayana, Indra, pleased by the hymns Vishvamitra taught him, frees Shunahshepa
edges.variation: Valmiki (Bala Kanda 62): the hymns are to Indra and Upendra, and the king is Ambarisha

edges.label: Asamanja was Sagara's son by Queen Keshini
Bhrigu granted Sagara one son to continue his line by one queen and sixty thousand sons by the other (Valmiki)
The Bhargava Chyavana blessed Sagara's mother, and the child was born safely despite the poison given her (Valmiki)
edges.variation: In the Puranas the sage who protects the mother and raises Sagara is Aurva

edges.label: Indra stole Sagara's sacrificial horse and hid it in the underworld beside Kapila
Vashishtha persuaded Sagara to spare the conquered Shakas, Yavanas and others and impose distinctive dress on them instead (Vishnu Purana)
Kapila burned Sagara's sixty thousand sons to ashes when they attacked him as the horse-thief
Anshuman was Asamanja's son and became Sagara's heir
Dilipa was the son of Anshuman
Pleased by Anshuman's reverence, Kapila returned the horse and told him how to save his uncles
Garuda, brother of Queen Sumati, told Anshuman that only the Ganga could purify the ashes (Valmiki)
Bhagiratha was the son of Dilipa, son of Anshuman
Vashishtha told the childless Dilipa to serve the cow Nandini (Raghuvamsha)
edges.variation: This concerns Kalidasa's Dilipa, father of Raghu, usually taken as a later king than Bhagiratha's father

edges.label: Surabhi cursed Dilipa to be childless after he passed her without saluting her (Raghuvamsha)
edges.variation: Kalidasa's Dilipa

edges.label: Dilipa served Nandini as a cowherd and offered his own body to a lion to save her, and she granted him a son
edges.variation: Kalidasa's Raghuvamsha, cantos 1–2

edges.label: Raghu descends from Bhagiratha in the Solar line
edges.variation: Valmiki: Bhagiratha - Kakutstha - Raghu. The Vishnu Purana and Bhagavata put Raghu several generations later, as son of Dirghabahu, son of Khatvanga-Dilipa. Kalidasa makes Raghu the son of Dilipa and Sudakshina

edges.label: Bhagiratha worshipped Shiva for a year, standing on one toe, so that Shiva would break the Ganga's fall
Bhagiratha brought the Ganga down to earth and led her to the ashes of his ancestors, so she is called Bhagirathi
Pleased by his austerities at Gokarna, Brahma granted Bhagiratha the descent of the Ganga
Shiva caught the falling Ganga in his locks and released her in streams at Bhagiratha's request
Aja was the son of Raghu (Kalidasa, Vishnu Purana)
edges.variation: Valmiki's genealogy makes Aja the son of Nabhaga, several generations after Raghu

edges.label: Kubera rained gold into Raghu's treasury overnight so that he could pay Kautsa's fee (Raghuvamsha)
Young Raghu fought Indra to recover Dilipa's stolen sacrificial horse (Raghuvamsha, canto 3)
edges.variation: Indra, impressed, granted him the merit of the sacrifice though he kept the horse

edges.label: Vashishtha served as Raghu's family priest
Dasharatha, father of Rama, was the son of Aja
Indumati chose Aja at her svayamvara in Vidarbha (Raghuvamsha)
Vashishtha consoled the grieving Aja, revealing that Indumati had been a cursed apsara (Raghuvamsha, canto 8)
Indumati was the mother of Dasharatha (Raghuvamsha)
edges.variation: The epics do not name Dasharatha's mother. This comes from Kalidasa

edges.label: Ila was born from Manu's sacrifice for a child and was later changed into the male Sudyumna
edges.variation: In the Shatapatha Brahmana Ida rises from Manu's offering after the flood

edges.label: In the Valmiki Ramayana, King Ila is the son of Kardama Prajapati
edges.variation: Uttara Kanda 87. Other texts make Ila Manu's child

edges.label: Budha, son of the Moon, fell in love with Ila while she was in female form
Vashishtha turned Manu's daughter Ila into the son Sudyumna and later interceded with Shiva for him
Shiva's decree that any man entering his grove would become female turned Sudyumna into Ila
At Vashishtha's plea, Shiva allowed Sudyumna to be a man one month and a woman the next (Bhagavata)
In the Ramayana, Uma granted half of Ila's plea, so that he would be a man and a woman in alternate months
Ila bore Pururavas to Budha, so the Lunar line is called Aila
Pururavas was the son of Budha, son of Soma
The apsara Urvashi lived with Pururavas on conditions, left him, and returned to him once a year (Rig Veda 10.95)
Ayu was the eldest son of Pururavas and Urvashi
Pururavas kindled the sacred fire with the fire-drills and established it in threefold form (Shatapatha Brahmana, Bhagavata)
Pururavas fought for Indra's side and rescued Urvashi from the demon Keshin (Vikramorvashiyam)
edges.variation: Found in Kalidasa's play and later sources

edges.label: Urvashi was the mother of Ayu
Nahusha was the eldest son of Ayu
Dattatreya, pleased by Ayu's patient service, blessed him with a son, Nahusha (Padma Purana)
Yayati was the son of Nahusha
Nahusha married Ashokasundari, daughter of Shiva and Parvati, after killing the demon Hunda (Padma Purana)
edges.variation: Found only in the Padma Purana

edges.label: Kicked by Nahusha while carrying his palanquin, Agastya cursed him to fall from heaven as a python
edges.variation: In the Anushasana Parva, Bhrigu hides in Agastya's hair and gives the curse

edges.label: Hidden in Agastya's matted hair, Bhrigu cursed the arrogant Nahusha (Mahabharata, Anushasana Parva)
edges.variation: Most versions give the curse to Agastya alone

edges.label: As Indra-regent, Nahusha demanded Shachi, who tricked him into his downfall
Nahusha occupied Indra's throne while Indra hid in a lotus stalk after killing Vritra
As a python, Nahusha seized Bhima and held him powerless (Vana Parva)
Yudhishthira's answers to the python's questions ended Nahusha's curse and freed Bhima
Yayati pulled Devayani out of a well by her right hand and married her
Yayati secretly married Sharmishtha, Devayani's servant, and fathered three sons with her
Yadu was Yayati's eldest son, born of Devayani
Puru was Yayati's youngest son, born of Sharmishtha
Shukracharya cursed Yayati with early old age for breaking his promise to Devayani
Shukracharya relented enough to let Yayati pass his old age to a willing son
Yayati cursed Yadu's line never to hold sovereign kingship because Yadu refused his old age
Yayati gave Puru back his youth and made him heir to the central kingdom over his elder brothers
Indra threw Yayati down from heaven when he boasted that no one equalled his austerities (Adi Parva 88)
Devayani was the beloved daughter of Shukracharya, preceptor of the asuras
Devayani was the mother of Yadu and Turvasu
Devayani and Sharmishtha quarrelled bitterly; Sharmishtha threw her into a well and later had to serve her
Rejected by Kacha, Devayani cursed him that the Mritasanjivani would never work for him
Kacha cursed Devayani in return that no brahmin would marry her
Sharmishtha was the mother of Druhyu, Anu and Puru
Shukracharya threatened to abandon the asuras and so forced Sharmishtha into servitude to Devayani
Kacha was the son of Brihaspati, preceptor of the gods
Shukracharya taught Kacha the Mritasanjivani, the knowledge of reviving the dead, while Kacha was inside his belly
The gods, led by Indra, sent Kacha to learn the Mritasanjivani from Shukracharya
Yadu and Puru were half-brothers, sons of Yayati by Devayani and Sharmishtha
Shurasena, grandfather of Krishna, descends from Yadu through Kroshtu and the Vrishnis
The Haihaya king Kartavirya Arjuna descends from Yadu's son Sahasrajit
The avadhuta Dattatreya taught King Yadu about his twenty-four gurus (Bhagavata, Canto 11)
Dushyanta was a king of the Paurava line founded by Puru
edges.variation: The Mahabharata and the Puranas list the intervening kings differently

edges.label: Dushyanta married Shakuntala by the gandharva rite in Kanva's hermitage
Bharata (Sarvadamana) was the son of Dushyanta and Shakuntala
Dushyanta fought the demons on Indra's behalf (Abhijnanashakuntalam, Act 7)
edges.variation: From Kalidasa's play, not the Mahabharata

edges.label: The sage Marica (Kashyapa) reunited Dushyanta with Shakuntala and their son in his celestial hermitage and blessed them (Kalidasa)
edges.variation: From Kalidasa's play, not the Mahabharata

edges.label: Shakuntala was born to Vishvamitra and the apsara Menaka
Menaka, sent by Indra to break Vishvamitra's austerities, bore Shakuntala and left her by the Malini
Kanva found the abandoned infant, named her, and raised her in his hermitage as a foster-daughter
Durvasa, ignored by the lovesick Shakuntala, cursed her to be forgotten by the man she was thinking of
edges.variation: From Kalidasa's Abhijnanashakuntalam, not the Mahabharata

edges.label: Shakuntala raised Bharata in Kanva's hermitage and presented him at Dushyanta's court
Kuru, son of Samvarana, descends from Bharata through Bhumanyu, Suhotra, Hastin and Ajamidha
edges.variation: The Puranas route the line through Bharata's adopted son Bharadvaja (Vitatha)

edges.label: Pleased by his Marutstoma sacrifice, the Maruts gave the heirless Bharata an adopted son, Bharadvaja (Puranas)
Bharata adopted Bharadvaja, renamed Vitatha, as his heir (Vishnu Purana, Bhagavata)
edges.variation: The Mahabharata gives Bharata a natural son, Bhumanyu, and does not mention the adoption

edges.label: Bharata was born and raised in Kanva's hermitage, where the sage performed his childhood rites
Pratipa, father of Shantanu, descends from Kuru
Indra granted Kuru that all who die on the field he ploughed would reach heaven, and so it became Kurukshetra
Kuru's mother Tapati was the daughter of Surya, so Surya was his maternal grandfather (Adi Parva)
